items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper examines the long-term exploitation of biotic and abiotic resources for personal ornament production at the cave of Arangas (Asturias, Spain). The site provides a valuable diachronic framework to assess continuity and change in the use of different raw materials across an exceptional stratigraphic sequence spanning from ca. 11,200 to 1600 cal BC.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    Although located approximately 11 km from the present-day coastline, and despite the topographic constraints on access, marine gastropods, particularly
                    <jats:italic>Trivia</jats:italic>
                    sp. and
                    <jats:italic>Tritia reticulata</jats:italic>
                    , represent the dominant raw materials throughout the sequence. Their persistent use suggests that the significance of marine materials was not directly dependent on proximity to the coast or their role in subsistence. The analysis considered all 51 personal ornaments recovered from the stratigraphic sequence, including freshwater gastropods, mammal teeth, bone, mineral, and undetermined biotic materials. By integrating stratigraphic, taxonomic, morphometric and technological analyses, including stereomicroscopy, experimental replication of perforation techniques, and micro-XRF elemental characterization of mineral ornaments, this study examines long-term patterns in raw material selection, manufacture and use from the Azilian to the Middle Bronze Age. Specifically, it suggests that marine resources may have maintained a symbolic relevance across the sequence, alongside variability in technical practices.
                  </jats:p>

items.title: Change and continuity in ornament production from the Azilian to the Bronze Age: the long-term stratigraphy of Arangas Cave, Spain

items.abstract: This article explores Acheulean handaxe variation worldwide through integration of known patterns of hominin biogeography with a geometric morphometric analysis of handaxe shape.Previous research has documented clear differences in handaxe shape between continental regions, but the mechanisms by which these patterns appeared have been dramatically underexplored.This paper illustrates how the worldwide distribution of handaxe shape can only be understood through the lens of repeated dispersal and differential exposure to climatic-driven extinction risk in different regions of the Acheulean world.The paper is the first shape-based analysis of handaxe shape using specimens across its entire latitudinal range, to explore how population instability is reflected in discontinuity of handaxe forms in those regions, especially in Northern Africa and northwestern Europe.This is combined with an examination of the factors that govern investment in artefactual symmetry and thinning, even when functionally unnecessary, to explore how regional continuity and social network formation are reflected in the toolkit.These findings have important implications for how we consider human movement over the last million years, and the conditions under which competition between different hominin lineages can be generated.

items.title: What shapes shape? Extinctions as a key driver of Acheulean cultural variation

items.abstract: The An-Nafud sand sea formed during the Pleistocene and occupies approximately 60,200 km 2 of northern Saudi Arabia. The erg has regional significance within the North African – Arabian Pleistocene desert trend, recording aeolian system development and early hominin migrations, while the underlying geology represents the poorly-documented Ediacaran and Paleozoic history of the northern sector of the Arabian plate. Reflection seismic data and deep wells have been used to establish the first description of the 3D geometry of this erg and the tectonostratigraphy of the underlying bedrock geology. The total volume of the erg is calculated at 9,399 km 3 , equivalent to 17.4 trillion tons of sand. The erg infills a cuesta topography eroded into gently-dipping Paleozoic strata. A widespread lake deposit is interpreted within the erg from reflection seismic, and relationships between major units within the erg include Late Pleistocene lake beds with hominin footprints overlain by 100 m - scale megadunes. A subcrop map to the erg establishes continuity of the pre-Pleistocene formation boundaries that trend away from the erg margins. A system of extensional faults with up to 1 km throw mapped within the Paleozoic strata is part of a more extensive trend associated with Red Sea rifting. One fault appears to offset the base of the erg by 125 m and related seismicity may have impacted Pleistocene hominins. The top of Precambrian basement occurs at depths of up to 6 km, infilling Ediacaran paleotopography that causes the oldest Paleozoic strata to onlap and differentially compact over features interpreted as eroded, castellated Precambrian granitic plutons.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Penaeoidea shrimps exhibit substantial diversity in reproductive morphology, but the evolutionary history of the male reproductive system (MRS) and its congruence with molecular phylogenies remain poorly understood. This study characterized MRS morphology across Penaeoidea and used these morphological data, together with a molecular phylogeny of the species analyzed herein, to reconstruct the ancestral states of MRS traits and investigate their evolutionary patterns and taxonomic implications. The MRS of 11 species was examined using histological methods, and phylogenetic analysis was conducted. In Benthesicymidae and Aristeidae, as well as in Solenoceridae and Penaeini, the median vas deferens (MVD) bears accessory and spermatic ducts, representing a synapomorphic trait and the putative plesiomorphic condition for Penaeoidea. In contrast, Trachypenaeini, Parapenaeini, and Sicyoniidae share a single duct in the MVD. Within Penaeini, the accessory gland is simple in
                    <jats:italic>Farfantepenaeus</jats:italic>
                    species but highly complex, with multiple glandular chambers, in
                    <jats:italic>Litopenaeus schmitti</jats:italic>
                    , supporting the separation of these lineages and arguing against treating
                    <jats:italic>Penaeus</jats:italic>
                    as a single genus. Benthesicymidae, Aristeidae, Solenoceridae, and Sicyoniidae lack accessory glands, representing a homoplastic condition, whereas Trachypenaeini and Parapenaeini exhibit a simplified accessory gland. The plesiomorphic spermatophore condition appears to be morphologically complex. Phylogenetic analyses recovered Penaeidae as paraphyletic, and substantial differences in MRS morphology among tribes support the hypothesis that these lineages may warrant elevation to family rank.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Fernanda C. Salti, Marcos Tavares, Caio S. Nogueira, Fernando J. Zara
